lessons.title: Creating lists and indexing
lessons.recap: Module 3 was all about strings. In its `split` lesson you met your first lists: `parts[0]` read a piece, `len(parts)` counted the pieces and `for p in parts:` looped over them. This module covers everything else a list can do.
lessons.what:
A **list** holds several values in order under one name. Each value is called an **item**. You read an item by its **index**, counting from 0, just as you read a character of a string.

There is one big difference from a string: a list can be changed after it is made. You can replace any item by assigning to its index.
lessons.why:
Without lists, every value needs its own variable, and you must know how many there are before you write the program:

```python
price1 = 4.5
price2 = 3.25
price3 = 10.0
```

With a list there is one name, any number of items, and a loop can visit them all:

```python
prices = [4.5, 3.25, 10.0]
```
lessons.syntax:
```python
prices = [4.5, 3.25, 10.0]    # square brackets, commas between the items
names = ["Ana", "Ben"]        # items can be any type
empty = []                    # a list with no items

len(prices)                   # 3      how many items
prices[0]                     # 4.5    the first item
prices[-1]                    # 10.0   the last item
prices[1] = 3.5               # replace the item at index 1
print(prices)                 # [4.5, 3.5, 10.0]
```

- The biggest index is `len(prices) - 1`, as with strings.
- Assigning to an index only works if that index already exists. It replaces an item. It never adds one.
- An index must be an `int`. A number typed by the user is text until you convert it.
- `print()` shows a list in square brackets. Strings inside it are shown with quotes.

examples.title: A list of prices
examples.code:
prices = [4.5, 3.25, 10.0]
print(prices)
print(len(prices))
print(prices[0])
print(prices[-1])
print(prices[0] + prices[1])
examples.explain:
- Printing the list shows every item inside square brackets.
- `prices[0]` is the first item and `prices[-1]` is the last.
- Each item is a normal value. Here they are floats, so `+` adds them.

examples.title: Replace an item
examples.code:
roster = ["Ana", "Ben", "Chloe"]
roster[1] = "Dev"
print(roster)
roster[-1] = roster[-1].upper()
print(roster)
print(len(roster))
examples.explain:
- `roster[1] = "Dev"` swaps out the second item. The other items do not move.
- `upper()` makes a new string. Assigning it back to `roster[-1]` stores it in the list.
- Replacing items never changes the length.

examples.title: Look up an item by a typed number
examples.code:
days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri"]
number = int(input("Day number (1 to 5): "))
print(days[number - 1])
examples.explain:
- People count from 1 and lists count from 0, so day 3 is at index 2.
- `int()` is needed because `input()` always gives text.

examples.title: The pieces from split are an ordinary list
examples.code:
row = "1042, Flat white ,4.50"
parts = row.split(",")
parts[1] = parts[1].strip()
parts[2] = float(parts[2])
print(parts)
print(parts[2] * 2)
examples.explain:
- `split` gives a list of strings. Because a list can be changed, each piece can be cleaned or converted and stored back.
- The printed list shows the types: `'1042'` has quotes, so it is still a string. `4.5` has none, so it is a number.

mistakes.title: An index one past the end
mistakes.fix: Read the last line first. `IndexError: list index out of range` means the position does not exist. Three items have indexes 0, 1 and 2. The last one is `days[2]` or `days[-1]`.
mistakes.error:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 2, in <module>
    print(days[3])
          ~~~~^^^
IndexError: list index out of range

mistakes.title: Assigning to an index that does not exist yet
mistakes.fix: The message says list **assignment** index out of range. An empty list has no index 0, so there is nothing to replace. Assigning to an index never makes a list longer. Adding items is done with `append`, which arrives in lesson 3.
mistakes.error:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 2, in <module>
    scores[0] = 7
    ~~~~~~^^^
IndexError: list assignment index out of range

mistakes.title: Round brackets where square ones belong
mistakes.fix: Round brackets after a name mean "call this", the way `print(...)` is called. A list cannot be called, so Python says `'list' object is not callable`. Indexing uses square brackets: `prices[0]`.
mistakes.error:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 2, in <module>
    print(prices(0))
          ~~~~~~^^^
TypeError: 'list' object is not callable

mistakes.title: Using typed text as an index
mistakes.fix: `"1"` is a string, and the message says indexes must be integers. This is what you get when you forget `int()` around `input()`. Write `days[int(choice)]`.
mistakes.error:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 3, in <module>
    print(days[choice])
          ~~~~^^^^^^^^
TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not str

lessons.remember: Square brackets make a list. Indexes start at 0, and the last one is len - 1.

quick_checks.code:
stock = [12, 0, 7]
stock[1] = stock[0] - 2
stock[0] = 0
print(stock)
print(stock[-1] + len(stock))
quick_checks.explain: `stock[1]` becomes `12 - 2`, which is `10`. That happens before `stock[0]` is set to `0`, so the order of the two lines matters. The last item is `7` and the length is `3`.

exercises.title: Opening hours
exercises.prompt: Read the code. Without running it, type exactly what it prints.
exercises.starter_code:
hours = [9, 9, 9, 9, 10, 0]
print(len(hours))
print(hours[0], hours[-1])
hours[-1] = hours[4] + 1
hours[1] = hours[1] - 1
print(hours)
print(hours[len(hours) - 2])
exercises.solution_explanation: The list has six items. `hours[0]` is `9` and `hours[-1]` is the last item, `0`. The last item is then replaced with `hours[4] + 1`, which is `11`, and the item at index 1 drops to `8`. `len(hours) - 2` is `4`, the second last index, which holds `10`.

exercises.title: First, last, count
exercises.prompt:
Read one line of names separated by commas. There are no spaces around the commas, and there is at least one name. Print the first name, the last name and how many names there are.

Example: for `Ana,Ben,Chloe`, print:

```
First: Ana
Last: Chloe
Count: 3
```
exercises.starter_code: line = input()

stdin_tests.name: one name is both first and last

hints: `split(",")` gives you the list.
The first item is at index 0. Which index is always the last item?
exercises.solution:
line = input()
names = line.split(",")
print("First:", names[0])
print("Last:", names[-1])
print("Count:", len(names))
exercises.solution_explanation: `split(",")` turns the line into a list. Index `0` is the first item and index `-1` is the last, however long the list is. With one name, both indexes point at the same item.

exercises.title: Month name
exercises.prompt:
This program reads a month number from 1 to 12 and should print the short name of that month. For `1` it should print `Jan`. It prints `Feb`. For `12` it crashes:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 3, in <module>
    print(months[number])
          ~~~~~~^^^^^^^^
IndexError: list index out of range
```
exercises.starter_code:
months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"]
number = int(input())
print(months[number])
hints: People count months from 1. Where do list indexes start?
Month 1 lives at index 0. What is the rule that turns one into the other?
exercises.solution:
months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"]
number = int(input())
print(months[number - 1])
exercises.solution_explanation: The bug is an off-by-one error. Indexes start at 0, so month 1 is at index 0 and month 12 is at index 11. Using the month number as the index gave the next month along, and for 12 it asked for index 12, which does not exist. Subtract 1 from the number.

exercises.title: Change the menu
exercises.prompt:
The starter code has a menu of four drinks. Read a position from 1 to 4, then read a new drink name on the next line. Remove any spaces from the ends of the new name. Replace the drink at that position, then print the whole list with `print(menu)`.

Example: for `2` and then `Long black`, print:

```
['Flat white', 'Long black', 'Mocha', 'Chai']
```
exercises.starter_code: menu = ["Flat white", "Latte", "Mocha", "Chai"]
hints: Position 1 is index 0.
Assign to the index: `menu[index] = something`.
`menu[position - 1] = name.strip()`
exercises.solution:
menu = ["Flat white", "Latte", "Mocha", "Chai"]
position = int(input())
name = input().strip()
menu[position - 1] = name
print(menu)
exercises.solution_explanation: A list can be changed in place: assigning to `menu[index]` replaces that one item and leaves the rest alone. The position typed by the user counts from 1, so the index is one less.

exercises.title: Swap first and last
exercises.prompt:
This program reads a line of track names separated by commas. It should swap the first and the last track and print the tracks joined with commas again.

For `Intro,Verse,Outro` it should print `Outro,Verse,Intro`. It prints `Outro,Verse,Outro`.
exercises.starter_code:
line = input()
tracks = line.split(",")
tracks[0] = tracks[-1]
tracks[-1] = tracks[0]
print(",".join(tracks))

stdin_tests.name: one track stays where it is

hints: After line 3 runs, where is the name `Intro` stored?
Line 3 overwrites the first track before anything has saved it.
Copy the first track into a spare variable before you overwrite it.
exercises.solution:
line = input()
tracks = line.split(",")
first = tracks[0]
tracks[0] = tracks[-1]
tracks[-1] = first
print(",".join(tracks))
exercises.solution_explanation: The bug is a lost value. `tracks[0] = tracks[-1]` overwrites the first track, so by the next line both ends hold `Outro` and the old first track is gone. Saving it in a spare variable first keeps it safe until it is needed.

exercises.title: Explain the middle name
exercises.prompt: Read the code. In your own words, explain what it does, why each step is there, and what it prints. Mention any edge cases you can see.
exercises.starter_code:
line = "Ana,Ben,Chloe,Dev,Eli"
names = line.split(",")
middle = len(names) // 2
print(names[middle])
names[middle] = names[middle].upper()
print(names)
exercises.model_explanation:
The program finds the middle item of a list, prints it, then replaces it with an upper-case copy.

`split(",")` gives a list of five names. `len(names) // 2` is `5 // 2`, which is `2`. Whole-number division is used because an index must be an `int`. Index 2 is the third of five items, the true middle, so it prints `Chloe`.

`names[middle].upper()` makes a new string `CHLOE`. On its own that would change nothing, so the result is assigned back to `names[middle]`. The last line prints `['Ana', 'Ben', 'CHLOE', 'Dev', 'Eli']`.

Edge cases: with an even number of names there is no single middle. For four names, `4 // 2` is `2`, so it picks the second of the two middle names. An empty line does not crash, because `"".split(",")` gives a list holding one empty string.
checklist: Said len(names) // 2 gives index 2, the middle of five items
Said why // is used and not / (an index must be a whole number)
Said the upper-case result has to be assigned back into the list
Gave the output: Chloe, then the list with CHLOE in the middle
Mentioned what happens with an even number of names

exercises.title: Clean every field
exercises.prompt:
Read one line of fields separated by commas. The fields may have spaces around them. Remove the spaces from the ends of every field, storing each cleaned field back in the list. Then print the list with `print()`.

Example: for `milk, bread ,  eggs`, print:

```
['milk', 'bread', 'eggs']
```
exercises.starter_code:
line = input()
parts = line.split(",")

stdin_tests.name: an empty field stays as an empty string

hints: To change an item you need its index, so loop over `range(len(parts))`.
`parts[i].strip()` makes a clean copy. Where does the copy have to go?
`parts[i] = parts[i].strip()`
exercises.solution:
line = input()
parts = line.split(",")
for i in range(len(parts)):
    parts[i] = parts[i].strip()
print(parts)
exercises.solution_explanation: `strip()` returns a new string, so each result must be stored back at the same index. Looping over the indexes with `range(len(parts))` gives the position needed for that assignment.

exercises.title: Safe seat lookup
exercises.prompt:
The starter code has a list of five guests. Guest 1 is `Ana`. Read one line and remove the spaces from its ends.

- If it is not made of digits only, print `Not a number`. This covers a minus sign and an empty line too.
- If the number is not from 1 to 5, print `No seat` and the number, such as `No seat 6`.
- Otherwise print the seat and the guest, such as `Seat 3: Chloe`.

Use `len(guests)` for the upper limit, not a fixed 5.
exercises.starter_code: guests = ["Ana", "Ben", "Chloe", "Dev", "Eli"]
hints: Check the text first, convert second, check the range third.
`isdigit()` is False for an empty string and for `-1`.
A list index of `-1` does not crash. It quietly gives the last guest, so 0 must be rejected by your own check.
exercises.solution_explanation: The order is clean, check, convert, then check the range. The lower limit matters as much as the upper one: seat 0 becomes index `-1`, which is a legal index and would print the last guest with no error at all.

exercises.title: Restock a shelf
exercises.prompt:
A shop has four shelves, numbered 1 to 4. The list holds how many items are on each shelf. The program reads a shelf number, then an amount to add (the amount can be negative). It should print the updated list, or `No such shelf` if the shelf number is not from 1 to 4.

For `2` and `5` it should print `[12, 5, 7, 30]`.

It has **three** bugs. The first one stops it straight away:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 4, in <module>
    if shelf > len(stock):
       ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: '>' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'
```
exercises.starter_code:
stock = [12, 0, 7, 30]
shelf = input()
amount = int(input())
if shelf > len(stock):
    print("No such shelf")
else:
    stock[shelf] = stock[shelf] + amount
    print(stock)
hints: Read the last line of the traceback. What are the two types being compared?
Once the shelf is a number, try shelf 4. Which index does shelf 4 live at?
Try shelf 0. An index of -1 is legal, so the list will not stop you.
exercises.solution:
stock = [12, 0, 7, 30]
shelf = int(input())
amount = int(input())
if shelf < 1 or shelf > len(stock):
    print("No such shelf")
else:
    stock[shelf - 1] = stock[shelf - 1] + amount
    print(stock)
exercises.solution_explanation: Bug 1: `input()` gives a string, and a string cannot be compared with a number or used as an index, so the shelf must be converted with `int()`. Bug 2: shelves count from 1 but indexes from 0, so the index is `shelf - 1`. Bug 3: only the upper limit was checked. Shelf 0 would become index `-1` and silently change the last shelf, so the check also needs `shelf < 1`.

lessons.title: Slicing lists
lessons.recap: Last lesson: a list is made with square brackets, `items[0]` is the first item, `items[-1]` is the last, and `items[i] = value` replaces an item.
lessons.what: A **slice** copies a run of items out of a list into a new list. It uses the same `start:stop` rule you learned for strings: start is included, stop is not.
lessons.why:
Many tasks need part of a list: the top three scores, every row except the header, the last five log lines. Without slices you need a loop and index arithmetic. With a slice it is one short expression:

```python
top = scores[:3]
rows = lines[1:]
recent = log[-5:]
```
lessons.syntax:
```python
items[1:4]              # the items at indexes 1, 2 and 3
items[:3]               # the first three
items[3:]               # everything from index 3 to the end
items[-2:]              # the last two
items[1:-1]             # everything except the first and the last
items[::2]              # every second item
items[::-1]             # a reversed copy
items[:2] + items[3:]   # + joins two lists into one new list
```

- A slice is always a list, even when it holds one item or none.
- The original list is not changed.
- A slice that runs past the end is not an error. You just get fewer items.

examples.title: First, last and middle parts
examples.code:
scores = [91, 85, 78, 70, 64, 50]
print(scores[:3])
print(scores[3:])
print(scores[1:4])
print(scores[-2:])
print(scores)
examples.explain:
- `[:3]` and `[3:]` share the number 3, so together they cover the whole list with nothing repeated.
- `[1:4]` stops before index 4.
- The last line shows that `scores` itself is untouched.

examples.title: A slice never crashes
examples.code:
queue = ["Ana", "Ben"]
print(queue[:5])
print(queue[3:])
print(queue[1:2])
print(queue[1])
examples.explain:
- Asking for five items from a list of two gives the two that exist.
- A slice that starts past the end gives an empty list.
- `queue[1:2]` is a list holding one item. `queue[1]` is the item itself. Look at the brackets and quotes in the output.

examples.title: Steps, reversing and joining
examples.code:
days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri"]
print(days[::2])
print(days[::-1])
print(days[:1] + days[-1:])
print(days[2:] + days[:2])
examples.explain:
- A third number is the step. `[::2]` takes every second item and `[::-1]` walks backwards.
- `+` between two lists makes a new list with the items of both.
- The last line moves the first two days to the back. This is called rotating a list.

mistakes.title: Joining a list and a single item with +
mistakes.fix: `days[:1]` is a list, but `days[4]` is the string `"Fri"`. The message says only a list can be joined to a list. Use a slice on both sides, `days[:1] + days[4:]`, or wrap the item in brackets: `[days[4]]`.
mistakes.error:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 2, in <module>
    ends = days[:1] + days[4]
           ~~~~~~~~~^~~~~~~~~
TypeError: can only concatenate list (not "str") to list

mistakes.title: Stopping one too early
mistakes.fix: No error. It prints `[91, 85]`, which is two scores, not three. The stop index is not included, so the first three items are `scores[0:3]`, or simply `scores[:3]`. The number after the colon is how many you get when the start is 0.

mistakes.title: Treating a one-item slice as the item
mistakes.fix: `names[:1]` is the list `['ana']`, not the string `'ana'`. A list has no `upper` method. To get the item itself, use an index: `names[0]`.
mistakes.error:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 3, in <module>
    print(first.upper())
          ^^^^^^^^^^^
AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'upper'

lessons.remember: A slice is always a new list, and the stop index is never included.

quick_checks.explain: `t[1:3]` is indexes 1 and 2. `t[-1:]` is `[4]` and `t[:1]` is `[3]`, and `+` joins them. `t[2:10]` runs past the end, so it holds only the three items from index 2 on.

exercises.title: Bus stops
exercises.prompt: Read the code. Without running it, type exactly what it prints.
exercises.starter_code:
stops = ["Central", "Town Hall", "Museum", "Park", "Zoo"]
print(stops[1:3])
print(stops[:2])
print(stops[-2:])
print(stops[::2])
print(len(stops[4:9]))
exercises.solution_explanation: `stops[1:3]` takes indexes 1 and 2 and stops before 3. `[:2]` is the first two and `[-2:]` is the last two. `[::2]` takes every second item, starting with the first. `stops[4:9]` asks for more than there is, so it gives the one item that exists from index 4 on, and its length is 1.

exercises.title: Top three
exercises.prompt:
Read one line of names in finishing order, separated by commas with no spaces. Print the first three, separated by a comma and a space. If there are fewer than three names, print them all.

Example: for `Ana,Ben,Chloe,Dev`, print `Ana, Ben, Chloe`.
exercises.starter_code: line = input()
hints: Which slice gives the first three items?
A slice never crashes when the list is short, so no `if` is needed.
exercises.solution:
line = input()
names = line.split(",")
top = names[:3]
print(", ".join(top))
exercises.solution_explanation: `names[:3]` gives the first three items, or fewer if the list is shorter. A slice past the end is not an error, so the short cases need no special handling.

exercises.title: The last two pages
exercises.prompt:
This program reads a line of page names a visitor opened, separated by commas. It should print the last two, joined with a comma. If there is only one page, it should print that page.

For `login,search,pay,logout` it should print `pay,logout`. It prints `pay`.
exercises.starter_code:
line = input()
pages = line.split(",")
recent = pages[-2:-1]
print(",".join(recent))
hints: A slice stops just before its stop index. Which item does `-1` point at?
Leave the stop out to go all the way to the end.
exercises.solution:
line = input()
pages = line.split(",")
recent = pages[-2:]
print(",".join(recent))
exercises.solution_explanation: The stop index of a slice is never included, and `-1` is the last item, so `[-2:-1]` left the last item out. `[-2:]` has no stop and runs to the end. With one page it gives that one page.

exercises.title: Readings only
exercises.prompt:
A sensor sends one line of comma-separated fields. The first field is the day and the last field is a status word. Everything between them is a reading. Print only the readings, separated by single spaces.

Example: for `Mon,12,15,11,OK`, print `12 15 11`.

If there are no readings, print an empty line.
exercises.starter_code: line = input()
hints: You want everything except the first item and the last item.
Start at index 1. Which stop leaves out the last item?
exercises.solution:
line = input()
parts = line.split(",")
readings = parts[1:-1]
print(" ".join(readings))
exercises.solution_explanation: `parts[1:-1]` starts after the first item and stops before the last. With only two fields the slice is empty, and joining an empty list gives an empty string, so an empty line is printed.

exercises.title: Pages of results
exercises.prompt:
A search shows three results per page. This program reads the results on one line (separated by commas), then a page number. Page 1 is the first three results. It should print the results on that page, joined with commas. A page past the end prints an empty line.

For `ant,bee,cat,dog,eel,fox,gnu` and page `1` it should print `ant,bee,cat`. It prints `dog,eel,fox`.
exercises.starter_code:
line = input()
page = int(input())
results = line.split(",")
start = page * 3
print(",".join(results[start:start + 3]))
hints: Work out by hand which index page 1 should start at. Then page 2.
Page 1 starts at index 0, page 2 at index 3. What do you multiply by 3 to get those?
exercises.solution:
line = input()
page = int(input())
results = line.split(",")
start = (page - 1) * 3
print(",".join(results[start:start + 3]))
exercises.solution_explanation: The bug is an off-by-one error in the start index. Pages count from 1 but indexes count from 0, so page 1 must start at index 0. `(page - 1) * 3` gives 0, 3, 6 and so on. The slice copes with the short last page and with a page past the end without any extra code.

exercises.title: Explain the rotating roster
exercises.prompt: Read the code. In your own words, explain what it does, why each step is there, and what it prints. Mention any edge cases you can see.
exercises.starter_code:
roster = ["Ana", "Ben", "Chloe", "Dev"]
shift = 6
k = shift % len(roster)
rotated = roster[k:] + roster[:k]
print(rotated)
print(roster)
exercises.model_explanation:
The program rotates a list: the first `k` people move to the back and everyone else moves up.

`shift % len(roster)` is `6 % 4`, which is `2`. The remainder is used because rotating four people by four places puts them back where they started. So rotating by 6 is the same as rotating by 2.

`roster[k:]` is everyone from index 2 on: `['Chloe', 'Dev']`. `roster[:k]` is the first two: `['Ana', 'Ben']`. `+` joins the two slices into a new list.

It prints `['Chloe', 'Dev', 'Ana', 'Ben']` and then `['Ana', 'Ben', 'Chloe', 'Dev']`. The second line shows that slicing made copies and the original list was not changed.

Edge cases: if `shift` is 0, 4 or 8 then `k` is 0 and the list comes out in the same order. If the roster is empty, `len(roster)` is 0 and the `%` raises a `ZeroDivisionError`.
checklist: Said % keeps the shift inside the length of the list (6 becomes 2)
Said the two slices are the back part and the front part, joined with +
Gave the output: ['Chloe', 'Dev', 'Ana', 'Ben'] then the original order
Said the original list is not changed, because slices are copies
Mentioned an empty roster (division by zero) or a shift that is a multiple of the length

exercises.title: Odd and even positions
exercises.prompt:
Read one line of readings separated by spaces. There may be extra spaces. Print two lines:

1. the 1st, 3rd, 5th (and so on) readings, separated by single spaces
2. the 2nd, 4th, 6th (and so on) readings, separated by single spaces

Example: for `3 5 8 2 9`, print:


lessons.title: Changing lists: append, insert, remove, pop
lessons.recap: Last lesson: a slice such as `items[:3]` or `items[-2:]` copies part of a list into a new list, and `+` joins two lists. None of that changes the original list.
lessons.what:
Lists can grow and shrink. `append` adds an item at the end. `insert` adds one at a position you choose. `remove` deletes an item by its value. `pop` deletes an item by its position and hands it back to you.

These four **change the list itself**. This is called changing it **in place**. They do not give you a new list, which is the opposite of string methods such as `upper()`.
lessons.why:
You rarely know how many items there will be: the user keeps typing names, a file has an unknown number of lines. So the most common pattern in list code is: start with an empty list, then `append` inside a loop.

```python
names = []
for piece in line.split(","):
    names.append(piece.strip())
```
lessons.syntax:
```python
items = []
items.append("milk")      # add at the end
items.insert(0, "tea")    # add at index 0; the rest move along
items.remove("milk")      # delete the first item equal to "milk"
last = items.pop()        # delete the last item and hand it back
first = items.pop(0)      # delete the item at index 0 and hand it back
"tea" in items            # True or False, as with strings
```

- `append`, `insert` and `remove` hand back `None`, Python's value for "nothing". Never write `items = items.append(x)`.
- `remove` raises an error if the value is not there. Check with `in` first.
- `pop` raises an error on an empty list. Check `len(items) > 0` first.
- On a list, `in` looks for a whole item. `"an" in ["Ana", "Dan"]` is `False`.

exercises.title: Explain the undo list
exercises.prompt: Read the code. In your own words, explain what it does, why each step is there, and what it prints. Mention any edge cases you can see.
exercises.model_explanation:
The program keeps a list of actions and lets the most recent one be undone.

Any command that is not `undo` is added to the end of `actions` with `append`. An `undo` takes the last action off the list with `pop()`, which also hands that action back so it can be printed. Because `append` adds at the end and `pop()` removes from the end, the newest action is always the first one undone.

`pop()` on an empty list raises an `IndexError`, so the code checks `len(actions) > 0` first and prints a message when there is nothing left.

Step by step: `type A` and `type B` are added. The first `undo` prints `Undid type B`. `type C` is added. The next two undos print `Undid type C` and `Undid type A`. The list is now empty, so the last `undo` prints `Nothing to undo`. The final line prints `[]`.
checklist: Said append adds to the end and pop() removes from the end, so the newest action is undone first

Said the length check stops pop() from crashing on an empty list

lessons.title: Looping over lists
lessons.recap: Last lesson: `append` and `insert` add items, `remove` and `pop` take them out, and all four change the list in place. The key pattern was an empty list plus `append` inside a loop.
lessons.what: A `for` loop visits each item of a list in order. There are two forms. Use `for item in items:` when you only need the values. Use `for i in range(len(items)):` when you also need the position: to number the items, to compare neighbours, or to change an item.
lessons.why:
Almost every list task is a loop with one of four jobs inside it:

1. **Total**: add each item to a running total.
2. **Count**: add 1 each time an item passes a test.
3. **Best so far**: remember the largest (or smallest, or longest) item seen.
4. **Build**: append the items you want to a new list.

You used the first three on numbers and characters in Modules 2 and 3. They work the same way on lists. Once you can spot which job a question is asking for, the code almost writes itself.
lessons.syntax:
```python
for price in prices:              # each item in turn
    total += price

for i in range(len(prices)):      # each index in turn: 0, 1, 2, ...
    print(i + 1, prices[i])       # the position and the item
    prices[i] = prices[i] * 2     # changing an item needs its index

kept = []                         # build a new list from an old one
for price in prices:
    if price > 5:
        kept.append(price)
```

- In `for price in prices`, the name `price` holds a copy of each value. Assigning to it does not change the list.
- For "best so far", start with the first item, `items[0]`, not with 0.
- Before you divide by `len(items)`, make sure the list is not empty.

lessons.title: Searching, counting and sorting
lessons.recap: Last lesson: `for item in items:` visits the values and `for i in range(len(items)):` visits the positions. You wrote loops for totals, counts, the best item so far and filtered copies.
lessons.what: Python has ready-made tools for the most common list questions. `in` asks whether a value is there. `index` asks where. `count` asks how many times. `min`, `max` and `sum` give the smallest item, the largest item and the total. `sort` and `sorted` put the items in order.
lessons.why:
Last lesson you wrote these as loops, and each one took four or five lines. The built-in versions take one line and leave less room for mistakes:

```python
best = temps[0]
for t in temps:
    if t > best:
        best = t
```

becomes

```python
best = max(temps)
```

You still need a loop when there is a condition, such as "count the scores over 50".
lessons.syntax:
```python
"Ana" in names               # True or False
"Ana" not in names           # the opposite
names.index("Ana")           # index of the first match
names.count("Ana")           # how many items equal "Ana"

min(scores)   max(scores)    # the smallest and the largest item
sum(scores)                  # the total (numbers only)

scores.sort()                # sort THIS list, smallest first
scores.sort(reverse=True)    # largest first
ranked = sorted(scores)      # a NEW sorted list; scores is not changed
scores.reverse()             # flip THIS list back to front
```

- `index` raises an error if the value is missing. Check with `in` first.
- `sort()` and `reverse()` change the list and hand back `None`. `sorted()` hands back a new list.
- Strings sort like words in a dictionary, with every capital letter before every lower-case letter. As strings, `"10"` comes before `"9"`.
- `min` and `max` raise an error on an empty list. `sum` of an empty list is 0.

exercises.title: Explain the median
exercises.prompt: Read the code. In your own words, explain what it does, why each step is there, and what it prints. Mention any edge cases you can see.
exercises.starter_code:
times = [34, 28, 41, 30]
ordered = sorted(times)
n = len(ordered)
middle = n // 2
if n % 2 == 1:
    median = ordered[middle]
else:
    median = (ordered[middle - 1] + ordered[middle]) / 2
print(median)
print(times)
exercises.model_explanation:
The program finds the **median** of a list: the middle value once the values are in order.

`sorted(times)` makes a sorted copy, `[28, 30, 34, 41]`. A copy is used so that the original order of `times` is kept. The middle of a list only means something after sorting.

`n // 2` is the middle index. If `n` is odd, there is one middle item and that is the median. If `n` is even, there are two middle items, at `middle - 1` and `middle`, and the median is their average.

Here `n` is 4, so `middle` is 2. The two middle values are `ordered[1]` and `ordered[2]`: 30 and 34. Their average is `32.0`. It is a float because `/` always gives a float.

It prints `32.0` and then `[34, 28, 41, 30]`, the list in its original order.

Edge case: an empty list has `n` equal to 0, which is even, so the `else` branch runs and indexing the empty list raises an `IndexError`.
checklist: Said the list has to be sorted before the middle means anything
Said sorted() makes a copy, so times keeps its original order
Said odd lengths have one middle item and even lengths average the two middle items
Gave the output: 32.0, then [34, 28, 41, 30]
Mentioned that an empty list would crash

lessons.title: Tuples and unpacking
lessons.recap: Last lesson: `in`, `index` and `count` search a list, `min`, `max` and `sum` summarise it, `sort()` reorders it in place and `sorted()` hands back a sorted copy.
lessons.what:
A **tuple** is a fixed group of values, written with round brackets. You read it like a list, by index, but you cannot change it after it is made.

**Unpacking** copies the items of a tuple or a list into separate variables in one line: `x, y = point`.
lessons.why:
Some values belong together and do not change: a point `(x, y)`, a `(name, price)` pair, a start and end time. A tuple says "this is one record with a fixed shape". A list says "this is a collection that may grow".

Unpacking makes parsing easier to read. Compare:

```python
parts = line.split(",")
name = parts[0]
price = parts[1]
```

with

```python
name, price = line.split(",")
```
lessons.syntax:
```python
point = (3, 4)                 # a tuple: round brackets
point[0]                       # 3   index and slice like a list
len(point)                     # 2

x, y = point                   # unpacking: one name for each item
name, price = "Pen,1.50".split(",")    # it works on lists too
a, b = b, a                    # swap two values

rows = [("Pen", 1.5), ("Pad", 3.25)]   # a list of tuples
for name, price in rows:       # unpack each tuple as the loop goes
    print(name, price)

single = (5,)                  # a one-item tuple needs the comma
```

- The number of names must equal the number of items exactly.
- A tuple has no `append`, `remove` or `sort`, and you cannot assign to `point[0]`. To "change" a tuple, build a new one.
- `print()` shows a tuple in round brackets: `(3, 4)`.

mistakes.title: Trying to change a tuple
mistakes.fix: A tuple is immutable. Make a new one: `point = (5, point[1])`. If you need to change items often, the data should be a list.

mistakes.title: A one-item tuple without the comma
mistakes.fix: Brackets around one value are just brackets, as in `(2 + 3) * 4`. So `single` is the `int` 5, which has no length. The comma makes the tuple: `(5,)`.

exercises.title: Do the bookings clash?
exercises.prompt:
Two lines each hold a room booking as a start time and an end time: `09:00-10:30`. Times use the 24-hour clock, and each booking ends after it starts.

Print `Clash` if the two bookings overlap, and `No clash` if they do not. A booking that ends at the same minute the other one starts is **not** a clash.

Example: `09:00-10:30` and `10:00-11:00` clash. `09:00-10:00` and `10:00-11:00` do not.

A good plan: turn each booking into a tuple of two numbers, the start and the end in minutes after midnight.

one booking is inside the other
the second ends as the first starts

hints: Split at `-` and unpack into start and end. Split each of those at `:` and unpack into hours and minutes.
Minutes after midnight is `hours * 60 + minutes`. Compare numbers, not text.
Two bookings overlap when each one starts before the other one ends.
exercises.solution:
slots = []
for i in range(2):
    start, end = input().split("-")
    hours, minutes = start.split(":")
    start_minutes = int(hours) * 60 + int(minutes)
    hours, minutes = end.split(":")
    end_minutes = int(hours) * 60 + int(minutes)
    slots.append((start_minutes, end_minutes))
first, second = slots
if first[0] < second[1] and second[0] < first[1]:
    print("Clash")
else:
    print("No clash")
exercises.solution_explanation: Unpacking does the parsing in three short steps: line into start and end, each time into hours and minutes. Turning each time into one number makes the comparison simple. Two ranges overlap exactly when each starts before the other ends. Using `<` and not `<=` means bookings that only touch do not clash.

lessons.title: Nested lists
lessons.recap: Last lesson: a tuple is a fixed record in round brackets, and unpacking gives each item its own name, as in `name, price = line.split(",")` and `for name, price in menu:`.
lessons.what:
The items of a list can themselves be lists. A list of lists is called a **nested list**. It is how Python holds a table or a grid: the outer list holds the rows, and each row is a list of values.

`table[r]` is one whole row. `table[r][c]` is one value in that row.
lessons.why:
A lot of real data is a table: a timetable, a seating plan, a spreadsheet, the rows of a CSV file. With a nested list the whole table lives under one name, and two indexes reach any cell.

```python
lines = ["Ana,7,9", "Ben,8,6"]
table = []
for line in lines:
    table.append(line.split(","))
```

This is exactly the shape you will build when you read files in Module 8.
lessons.syntax:
```python
table = [
    ["Ana", 7, 9],
    ["Ben", 8, 6],
]
table[0]             # the first row: ['Ana', 7, 9]
table[0][1]          # row 0, column 1: 7
table[-1][-1]        # the last value of the last row: 6
len(table)           # the number of rows: 2
len(table[0])        # the number of values in row 0: 3

for row in table:            # each row is a list
    for value in row:        # each value in that row
        print(value)

table.append(["Chloe", 5, 5])    # add a whole row
table[1][2] = 10                 # change one value
```

- The row index comes first, then the column index.
- Rows are separate lists, so they can have different lengths. Use `len(row)`, not a fixed number.

lessons.title: Copying and mutation gotchas
lessons.recap: Last lesson: a nested list is a list of rows, and `table[row][column]` reaches one value. Rows are lists in their own right, so they can be looped over, summed and appended.
lessons.what:
A variable does not hold a list. It holds a **reference** to it: think of a name tag tied to the list. `b = a` ties a second name tag to the same list. It does not make a second list. The second name is called an **alias**.

To **mutate** a list means to change it in place, with `append`, `sort`, `items[0] = x` and so on. A change made through one name is seen through every other name of that list.
lessons.why:
This is behind some of the most confusing bugs in Python: "I changed my copy and the original changed too." It never came up with numbers and strings, because they cannot be changed in place. Lists can, so it matters whether two names mean one list or two.

```python
backup = scores        # one list, two names
backup = scores[:]     # two lists
```

Three places where it bites: a "backup" that is really an alias, removing items from a list while looping over it, and a grid whose rows are all the same list.
lessons.syntax:
```python
b = a                  # NOT a copy: two names, one list
b = a[:]               # a copy: a slice of the whole list
b = a.copy()           # a copy: the same thing, spelt out
b = sorted(a)          # a sorted copy; a.sort() would change a itself

for item in items[:]:              # loop over a copy when the loop removes items
    if item == "":
        items.remove(item)

grid = []                          # a grid needs a new list for every row
for r in range(3):
    grid.append([0] * 4)           # [0] * 4 is [0, 0, 0, 0]
```

- `[0] * 4` repeats the items of a list: it makes `[0, 0, 0, 0]`.
- `a[:]` and `a.copy()` copy the outer list only. In a nested list, the rows inside are still shared. Copy each row too if you need them separate.
- The methods that mutate: `append`, `insert`, `remove`, `pop`, `sort`, `reverse`, and assignment to an index. Slices, `sorted()` and `+` make new lists.

- The removals happen on the real list.
- Building a new list of the items to keep is just as good, and often clearer.

mistakes.title: Copying only the outside of a nested list

lessons.remember: b = a is a second name, not a second list. Copy with a[:].

`grid = [row, row]` does not hold two rows. It holds the one list `row` twice. So `grid[0][1] = 5` changes that one list, and both "rows" show the change. It prints `[[0, 5, 0], [0, 5, 0]]`.

`row.append(1)` changes the same list again, through its own name. The grid shows it in both places: `[[0, 5, 0, 1], [0, 5, 0, 1]]`.

`fixed = [row[:], row[:]]` uses slices, and each slice is a new list. The two rows of `fixed` are separate from each other and from `row`. So `fixed[0][0] = 7` changes only the first row. It prints `[[7, 5, 0, 1], [0, 5, 0, 1]]`.

The last line prints `[0, 5, 0, 1]`: `row` was not touched by the change to `fixed`.

The rule: a list inside another list is shared unless you copy it.
